data.title: Get involved
data.hero_subhead: Volunteer on a harvest day, mentor a new garden or join the seed library.

children.text: Harvest days run every other Saturday from June to October. Mentors meet a new garden once a week in its first season.

data.title: Apply now
data.hero_subhead: Tell us about the lot and the neighbors who want to grow there. We reply within two weeks.

children.text: The lot's address, who owns it if you know, and the names of five neighbors who will help. We read every application and set up a visit.
Fields marked * are required.
Everything a new garden needs in its first season, from a
soil test
to a watering rota.
Before anything goes in the ground, send a soil sample to the county extension office. City lots often hold lead from old paint and fuel.
Raised beds
Raised beds fix almost anything the test finds. Once they are built, set a watering rota before the first hot week.

data.title: Seed library
data.hero_subhead: Borrow seeds in spring and return saved seeds in fall, so the library grows every year.

children.text: Pick up to five packets each spring. In the fall, bring back seed saved from your best plants, labeled with the crop, variety and garden.
The library lives in the shed at the Elm Street garden, open Saturday mornings from April to October.
Reserve shovels, wheelbarrows and hoses for a work day. Pick up and return at the garden shed.

children.text: The tool share now has two more wheelbarrows, a broadfork and a second set of long-handled loppers, bought with donations from the spring plant sale.
Reserve them on the
tool share

children.text: The first hot week is when new gardens lose the most plants. A rota means every bed gets water, even when the regulars are away.
Setting one up
Pick one evening slot per person each week.
Water the soil, not the leaves, and water deeply.
Post the rota on the shed door and in the group chat.

children.text: Forty kids from three after-school programs planted, weeded and harvested at Elm Street, Maple Court and the Grove this summer.
Their favorite crop, by a wide margin, was the
purple bush beans

data.excerpt: Forty kids from three after-school programs spent the summer growing food at three gardens.
data.title: A summer of youth growers

children.text: Seven years ago the lot at Elm and 4th was a fenced square of gravel and broken glass. This September we weighed
1,140 pounds
of produce from it, and gave most of it away on the sidewalk.
None of that came from expertise. It came from showing up every Saturday, and from neighbors who noticed and started showing up too.
If you're thinking about a garden on your block, read the
starter guide
. It's everything I wish I'd known in year one.

data.excerpt: Seven years after the first raised bed, the Elm Street garden harvested more than half a ton of food this season.
data.title: Elm Street's best harvest yet

children.text: Saving seed is how the library grows. Every packet you return in the fall becomes three packets for someone else in the spring.
Start with the easy ones
Beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes are the best first crops to save from: they mostly pollinate themselves, so the seed grows true.
Let a few of the healthiest plants go fully to seed.
Harvest on a dry day and spread the seed on paper for a week.
Label everything: crop, variety, garden and year.
Bringing seed back
Drop labeled envelopes in the return box at any member garden, or bring them to the
seed library
swap on the first Saturday of November.

data.excerpt: Beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes are the easiest crops to save seed from. Here's how to bring your harvest back to the library.
data.title: How to save seed for the library

children.text: Bring saved seed, take home something new. The swap runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Saturday, November 7, in the Elm Street shed.
No seed to trade? Come anyway: first-time growers go home with five packets.
